summary: Defines an nfs URL scheme for naming files and directories on NFS servers, following the general URL syntax of RFC 1738. This lets such files be referred to in the same way as web or FTP resources. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It gives files on a shared network disk their own web-style address, so you can write one down and share it.

questions: how to refer to an nfs file with a url
how do i refer to an nfs file with a url
how does nfs work with urls
subtitle: A web-style address for files on shared network storage.

tldr.problem: Files on NFS servers are identified by server name and path, but there is no standard way to express them as URLs like web files or FTP files.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2224 defines the nfs:// URL scheme, which names NFS files just like HTTP and FTP files, using the server hostname, optional port, and a file path.
tldr.outcome: Network applications can now refer to NFS files using a unified URL syntax, making NFS more accessible and easier to share.

today: RFC 2224 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. NFS remains widely used for network storage, though WebNFS adoption has been limited due to the rise of HTTP-based file sharing and cloud storage.

sections.title: Introduction and URL Syntax
sections.content:
RFC 2224 defines the nfs URL scheme for referring to files and directories on NFS (Network File System) servers using a standard web-style address. The URL follows the pattern nfs://hostname:port/path, where the port is optional and defaults to 2049 (the NFS service port).

The syntax is based on the general URL syntax from RFC 1738, letting NFS files be referenced the same way as web pages, FTP files, and other network resources. Characters that are not allowed in the path component must be URL-encoded.
sections.eli5: An NFS URL looks like a website address but starts with 'nfs://' instead of 'http://'. It points to a file on a network disk that you and others can share.

sections.title: WebNFS: Efficient Access Method
sections.content:
To evaluate an NFS URL, the client uses the WebNFS method, which reduces the number of protocol messages needed and passes easily through firewalls and proxy servers. The client first tries to connect to the NFS server using TCP on the specified port; if the server refuses the TCP connection, the client falls back to UDP.

The client attempts to use NFS version 3; if the server returns an error indicating version 3 is not supported, the client retries with NFS version 2. This version negotiation is automatic and requires no manual configuration.
sections.eli5: WebNFS is the quick way to ask an NFS server for a file without a lot of back-and-forth messages. It tries to use the modern way first, and if that does not work, it falls back to the older way.

sections.title: Public Filehandle and Multi-component Lookup
sections.content:
NFS normally requires the client to obtain a filehandle from the server's mount protocol before accessing files. WebNFS simplifies this by using a public filehandle, a special reserved filehandle with zero value. For NFS version 2, the public filehandle is 32 zero octets; for version 3, it has zero length.

With the public filehandle, the client can perform a multi-component lookup: in a single LOOKUP request, it provides the entire path (for example, 'a/b/c') and the server returns the filehandle for the final component. This eliminates the need for separate LOOKUP requests for each path component and removes the need for the mount protocol altogether.
sections.eli5: The public filehandle is like a magic key that the server always recognizes. With it, you can ask for a whole file path in one request instead of asking 'where is a?', then 'where is b?', then 'where is c?'.

sections.title: Absolute and Relative Paths, Symbolic Links
sections.content:
In an NFS URL, the path normally starts with a single slash and is relative to the directory associated with the public filehandle on the server. A path starting with a double slash (//) is treated as absolute, evaluated from the server's filesystem root. Whether a symbolic link in an NFS URL resolves correctly depends on both the client and server; if a symbolic link contains an absolute path and the public filehandle is not associated with the server's root, the resolution may fail.

When a client retrieves a symbolic link, it sends a READLINK request to get the path the link points to, then combines that path with the original URL according to RFC 1808 relative URL rules. A symbolic link can even contain a complete URL to a different server or scheme.
sections.eli5: Regular paths find files relative to the public filehandle's directory. Paths starting with '//' find files from the server's root instead. Symbolic links (shortcuts) can point to other files or even other servers.

sections.title: Fallback and Mount Protocol
sections.content:
Some NFS servers do not support the public filehandle and multi-component lookup, or they return errors such as NFS3ERR_STALE when the client uses them. For such servers, the client can fall back to the traditional MOUNT protocol. The client determines which NFS version the server supports from earlier negotiation, then uses the appropriate version of the MOUNT protocol to obtain a filehandle for the requested path.

The MOUNT protocol uses the PORTMAP service to discover which port the server's mount daemon is listening on. After successfully mounting, the client should send an UNMOUNT request to prevent the server from accumulating a list of mounted filesystems.
sections.eli5: If the fancy public filehandle does not work, the client can fall back to asking the server's mount daemon the old-fashioned way. When done, it tells the server to forget about the mount so the server does not accumulate junk.
